| [LIT-139](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-139.md) v2 | Inductive Risk and Values in Science | Douglas (2000), DOI-10.1086/392855. Hempel's "inductive risk" (the chance of wrongly accepting or rejecting a hypothesis) arises at three internal stages of science: choosing a methodology such as a significance level, characterising data, and interpreting results. Wherever the non-epistemic consequences of error can be foreseen, weighing them requires non-epistemic values. Douglas shows this on dioxin cancer studies. Three pathologist panels (1978, 1980, 1990) scored the same Kociba rat-liver slides differently (e.g. 34/50, 33/47, 18/50 tumours at 100 ng/kg/day). Choosing between threshold and no-threshold readings of the same data has meant regulatory limits about 100× apart. Values enter only indirectly, through the consequences of error, never as evidence that a claim is true. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-145](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-145.md)); worth reading as the canonical, compact statement of the modern inductive-risk argument. | [LIT-187](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-187.md) v3 | On the Philosophy of Unsupervised Learning | Watson (2023), DOI-10.1007/s13347-023-00635-6. Watson argues that clustering, abstraction and generative modelling each come with an epistemic thesis (EC, EA, EG — we identify natural kinds, essential properties and unrealized possibilities via such algorithms or something like them), which he accepts. Each also comes with an ontological thesis (OC, OA, OG — these just *are* what the algorithms ought to find under ideal conditions), which he rejects because nothing guarantees they are effectively computable. He adds a pragmatic, context-relative view of natural kinds, and closes with the claim that unsupervised outputs are neither "objective" nor vacuous. To be a true believer is to be a system "whose behavior is reliably and voluminously predictable" by it. The choice of stance is free, but its success is objective: Laplacean Martians who skipped it would miss real patterns. Thermostat and person differ only by degree. Why the strategy works is answered easily by evolution, and not yet at all by mechanism. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-353](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-353.md)), in the revised text reprinted in Mind Design II (1997), not the 1981 printing; worth reading as Dennett's statement that belief is objective although only visible through a strategy: anything whose behaviour is "reliably and voluminously predictable" by the intentional strategy is a believer "in the fullest sense of the word". It turns the 1971 paper's observer-relativity ([LIT-440](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-440.md)) into "the facts about the success or failure of the stance … are perfectly objective", introduces the Martian thought experiment and the intentional "real patterns" later worked out in [LIT-220](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-220.md), and runs the thermostat-to-person continuum ("no magic moment"). Its criterion admits any system on which the strategy pays, groups included, but the essay never applies it to a group. |
| [LIT-411](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-411.md) | Could a Large Language Model be Conscious? | Chalmers (2023), arXiv:2303.07103; Boston Review, 9 August 2023; from a NeurIPS 2022 invited talk. Asks for a feature X that LLMs have (or lack) and that indicates consciousness (or its absence). Self-report, seeming-conscious, conversation and general intelligence give at most weak evidence for it. Biology, senses and embodiment, world and self models, recurrent processing, a global workspace and unified agency are the evidence against. All but biology are temporary. On mainstream assumptions: under 10% credence for current LLMs, 25% or more for conscious LLM+ systems within a decade. Twelve challenges are offered as roadmap or red flags. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-345](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-345.md)), from arXiv v3 (the Boston Review text), with v1's conclusions compared; worth reading as the clearest short statement of the case for and against consciousness in LLMs, and as the origin of the "theory-balanced" credence approach that Butlin et al. built on. Its method is a regimented request for a feature X, and its verdicts are credences offered "for illustrative purposes": under 10% for current LLMs, 25% or more for conscious LLM+ systems within a decade, on "mainstream assumptions". It does not break the deadlock [THEORY-023](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-023.md) describes. It is an instance of it: mimicry undercuts self-report, the main obstacles are theory-derived, and biology is set aside rather than answered. |
| [LIT-421](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-421.md) | Foreword | Chalmers (2008), DOI-10.1093/acprof:oso/9780195333213.002.0007. The co-author's retrospective on the extended mind: his iPhone is "part of my mind already". The one principled objection is that perception and action bound the mental. His reply is revisionist and contextualist: whether Otto's belief counts as extended flips with explanatory purpose. No Otto-style twin case works for consciousness, so he tentatively keeps an internal conscious core. The thesis needs only a weak, parity-style functionalism and is compatible with dualism. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-369](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-369.md)); worth reading as the shortest statement of where Chalmers stands on the thesis he co-authored, ten years on. Three things in eight pages: the iPhone as a present-day Otto's notebook; the perception-action boundary as the one principled objection, answered by explanatory revisionism and a "Necker cube" view on which whether Otto's belief is extended depends on explanatory purpose; and a tentative internal "conscious core", resting on the failure of any Otto-style twin case for consciousness. It is a foreword: every position is stated briefly and several are offered as "perhaps". |
| [LIT-425](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-425.md) | The Meta-Problem of Consciousness | Chalmers (2018), Journal of Consciousness Studies 25(9–10):6–61. The meta-problem is to explain, in terms that do not mention consciousness, why we judge that consciousness poses a hard problem. It is an "easy" problem with an empirical programme. Of thirteen candidate mechanisms, the most promising is an introspective model that attributes primitive relations of awareness to primitive qualities, with a sense of acquaintance. A realist theory should explain how its basis of consciousness produces these judgments, which IIT and biological theories struggle to do. Debunking arguments for illusionism can be blocked, but a residual sense of coincidence remains. Only strong illusionism dissolves the hard problem, and it is false because people feel pain. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-354](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-354.md)); worth reading as the statement of the meta-problem, explaining in topic-neutral terms why we judge that consciousness poses a hard problem, and as a survey of thirteen candidate mechanisms. Cite it for four things: the meta-problem as an "easy" problem with a research programme; the meta-problem challenge to theories of consciousness, which tells against IIT and biological theories; the analysis of debunking and coincidence arguments for illusionism; and the argument that only strong illusionism dissolves the hard problem, with a Moorean rejection of strong illusionism. Its own preferred solution is offered as "closer to a fleshed-out explanandum" than an explanation. |
| [LIT-430](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-430.md) v2 | The Intentional Stance | Dennett (1987), MIT Press. Per its publisher, the "first full-scale presentation of a theory of intentionality" Dennett had been developing for almost twenty years: we understand each other by adopting a stance, "a predictive strategy of interpretation that presupposes the rationality" of whatever we predict. Six chapters reprint papers of the 1980s, each followed by a new "Reflections" essay; the first and the last three chapters are new. Chapter 2 is True Believers ([LIT-398](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-398.md)). Unread: registered from the description and a catalogue's contents note. | Unavailable — registered 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and a library catalogue's contents note, not read: no lawful full text of the book could be reached. The Internet Archive scans are lending-only (access-restricted, printdisabled), the MIT Press page and loc.gov were blocked, and the Tufts Digital Library holds earlier versions of several chapters as papers but not the book. Its chapter 2 is True Believers ([LIT-398](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-398.md)), read in full in its 1997 reprint, which is the revised book text. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-433](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-433.md) | Quining Qualia | Dennett (1988), in Marcel & Bisiach (eds.), Consciousness in Contemporary Science, OUP, pp. 42–77. Qualia as tradition has them are ineffable, intrinsic, private and directly apprehensible, and fifteen intuition pumps argue that nothing has all four. Two neurosurgical routes to an apparent colour inversion, one changing qualia and one only memory-linked reactions, feel the same from the inside. So the subject cannot know his own qualia better than an outside tester can. What is real is practical ineffability and idiosyncrasy: we refer to information-rich public properties through our own detectors of them. Hence "there simply are no qualia at all". | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-357](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-357.md)); worth reading as the founding statement of qualia eliminativism and the source of the post-Cartesian side in the record's consciousness readings. It argues by fifteen intuition pumps, not by proof, and says so. Its lasting results are two: the alternative-neurosurgery and Chase-and-Sanborn cases, which show that neither the subject nor the physiologist can separate a change in qualia from a change in reactions to them; and a positive account of practical ineffability and privacy as idiosyncratic, information-rich property detection. Its conclusion, "there simply are no qualia at all", is a tactical choice of words by the author's own endnote 2, not a stronger thesis than that. |
| [LIT-440](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-440.md) | Intentional Systems | Dennett (1971), Journal of Philosophy 68(4):87–106. An Intentional system is one whose behaviour can be explained and predicted by ascribing beliefs and desires and assuming rationality, which is the Intentional stance beside the design and physical stances. Being one is relative to an observer's strategy, and the choice of stance is pragmatic. The stance is "unmetaphysical": it sets aside composition, consciousness and moral standing. As psychology it is vacuous, because it presupposes rationality. Any theory that gives content to a part takes out a "loan of intelligence", repayable only by analysing away the part's reader: "there a little man is concealed". | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-350](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-350.md)); worth reading as the first statement in print of the intentional stance and of the homunculus debt that Dennett later answers with "discharge". Its definition makes being an Intentional system relative to an observer's predictive strategy, and it says outright that the definition "does not say that Intentional systems really have beliefs and desires" (p. 91). True Believers ([LIT-398](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-398.md)) later withdraws exactly that relativity. Its lasting tool for this record is the "loan of intelligence" (p. 96): any theory that gives a part content owes an account of that part's reader, and "wherever a theory relies on a formulation bearing the logical marks of Intentionality, there a little man is concealed". The paper does not treat a group as an Intentional system. |
| [LIT-451](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-451.md) | Of Personal Identity | Hume (1739), Treatise 1.4.6, with the Appendix (1740). There is no impression of a self, "constant and invariable", so no idea of one: introspection finds only "some particular perception or other", and the mind is "a bundle or collection of different perceptions". The identity we ascribe to it is "fictitious", like that of plants, ships and churches: an easy transition of the imagination along resemblance and causation, with memory discovering rather than producing it, so that hard cases are "grammatical" rather than philosophical. The Appendix retracts the account of the connecting principle: two principles he cannot reconcile or renounce leave the matter "too hard for my understanding". | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-386](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-386.md)), in the Merivale–Millican critical text on davidhume.org, with the Appendix's second thoughts (App. 10–21); worth reading as the founding statement of the bundle view and the first published retraction of it. The section finds no impression of a self, calls the mind "a bundle or collection of different perceptions", and explains our ascription of identity to it as a fiction of the imagination run on resemblance and causation, the same fiction that makes a repaired ship or a rebuilt church "the same". The Appendix then confesses that it cannot explain what unites the perceptions and leaves the problem "too hard for my understanding". The section's case is introspective and associationist; its Appendix is the clearest statement of what any bundle view owes. |
| [LIT-458](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-458.md) | Illusionism as a Theory of Consciousness | Frankish (2016), Journal of Consciousness Studies 23(11–12):11–39, the target article of the issue later published as Illusionism as a Theory of Consciousness (2017). Names "illusionism": phenomenal properties are not instantiated, and the task is the "illusion problem" of explaining why experiences seem to have them. Strong illusionism (no phenomenal properties at all, only "quasi-phenomenal" physical ones introspection misrepresents) is separated from weak illusionism (real phenomenal properties that merely seem ineffable, intrinsic, private), which it argues collapses into the strong form or into radical realism. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-384](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-384.md)); worth reading as the founding statement of illusionism under that name, and the target article that Dennett's "Illusionism as the Obvious Default Theory of Consciousness" ([LIT-434](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-434.md)) answers. It names the "illusion problem", draws the strong/weak illusionism line with "quasi-phenomenal" properties, and argues from conservatism, anomalousness and the debunking argument that strong illusionism should be the research programme. It states a programme, not a theory: by its own account it "will not propose a detailed illusionist theory" (p. 1 of the eprint), and its positive arguments are abductive and openly so. |
| [LIT-470](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-470.md) v2 | Foundations for a Social Ontology | Thomasson (2003), ProtoSociology 18–19:269–290. Per its abstract: the social world poses a metaphysical puzzle (how facts and objects created by human intentionality can be real) and an epistemological one (how such products can include objective facts for the social sciences to discover). Searle's account in The Construction of Social Reality is too narrow to solve either; rules for constructing social reality that parallel rules for make-believe give a more comprehensive ontology, but talk of social reality is not pretence. Unread: filed from the abstract. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's abstract; no lawful full text was reachable (the Philosophy Documentation Center sells it at $20, PhilPapers returned 403, and the Academia.edu copy sits behind a bot check), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. By its abstract it argues that Searle's account of social facts is too narrow and that rules modelled on the rules of make-believe give a fuller social ontology; how, is not recorded here. |
| [LIT-474](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-474.md) v2 | The Social Construction of Reality: A Treatise in the Sociology of Knowledge | Berger & Luckmann (1966), Doubleday. A treatise in the sociology of knowledge. By its contents: the reality of everyday life and its language; society as objective reality (institutionalization, sedimentation and tradition, roles, legitimation, symbolic universes); society as subjective reality (primary and secondary socialization, identity). Unread: filed from catalogue records and the table of contents only. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-02 from library catalogue records and the 1966 edition's table of contents; no lawful full text was reachable (the book is in copyright, the Internet Archive scans of the 1966 Doubleday edition and a 1967 printing are lending-only, and there is no author-posted text), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. It is the sociology-of-knowledge treatise whose title phrase [ADR-017](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-017.md)'s topic blurb uses; what it claims, beyond its contents page, is not recorded here. |
| [LIT-485](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-485.md) v2 | The Construction of Social Reality | Searle (1995), Free Press, New York (xiii + 241 pp.). The founding book of Searle's social ontology. Per its catalogue description, it argues that some facts are independent of human observers and some require human agreement. Its chapters move from the building blocks of social reality and the creation of institutional facts through language and a general theory of institutional facts, to a defence of external realism and the correspondence theory of truth. Unread: filed from the catalogue record and contents; the record reads the theory in Searle's 2006 restatement. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-02 from catalogue records and a library scan of the table of contents; no lawful full text was reachable (the book is in print with Free Press / Simon & Schuster, the Internet Archive copies are either lending-only or unauthorised uploads, and Searle posted no draft), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. The record reads the theory through Searle's own 2006 restatement ([LIT-482](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-482.md), read in full), which is the entry to start from. |
| [LIT-492](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-492.md) v2 | On Social Facts | Gilbert (1989), Routledge (reissued by Princeton University Press, 1992; DOI-10.1515/9780691214627). The book asks whether social groups are real over and above individuals' thoughts. It analyses everyday concepts of social action, social groups, collective belief and social convention, in dialogue with Weber, Simmel, Durkheim and David Lewis, and proposes that core social phenomena are "plural subject" phenomena. Unread: filed from the publishers' descriptions and the chapter list. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-02 from the publishers' records and the chapter list; no lawful full text was reachable (the Princeton reissue is sold as an e-book on De Gruyter, and the Internet Archive's copy of the Routledge edition is lending-only), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. It is Gilbert's book-length treatment of plural subjects, collective belief and social convention; "Walking Together" ([LIT-477](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-477.md)) is the short version. |
| [LIT-639](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-639.md) | The Harder Problem of Consciousness | Block (2002), The Journal of Philosophy 99(8):391–425. For anyone who is both a naturalist (physicalism is the default) and a phenomenal realist (consciousness is real and not defined by function), a merely superficial functional isomorph of us with a different physical basis, "Commander Data", poses a harder problem than the hard one. We have no conception of evidence that could show whether he is conscious, so physicalism is the default yet inaccessible, and it is the subjective default that he is not conscious though the question is open. Disjunctive or functional bases would save naturalism but could never be known. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-501](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-501.md)); worth reading as the argument that whether a functional duplicate of us made of different stuff is conscious is not just unknown but "meta-inaccessible": we have no conception of evidence that would settle it. For a naturalist who is also a phenomenal realist, physicalism is the default and yet whether such a being is conscious cannot bear on it. The paper also dissolves one form of the hard problem by treating subjective and objective as properties of concepts, not of properties. It lays out the tension and argues for no way out. |
| [LIT-716](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-716.md) | Network Epistemology: Communication in Epistemic Communities | Zollman (2013), Philosophy Compass 8:15–27. A survey of how communication structure affects group learning. No structure is best for all problems. With costly lossless transmission, minimally connected networks are optimal; with lossy transmission, stars. When agents average opinions, regular networks are best and denser is faster. In bandit problems minimally connected networks are best even when communication is free. Optimal networks may not be reached by individuals' choices. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-567](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-567.md)): read in full from the author's posted manuscript. Worth reading as the short survey of network epistemology up to 2012. Its main lesson is that the best communication structure depends on the learning problem. Pooling estimates favours dense, regular networks. Costly transmission favours sparse ones, often a star. Active learning in bandit problems favours minimally connected ones. Intuitions about "too little" or "too centralized" communication are often wrong. A survey, weighed as one. |
| [LIT-717](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-717.md) v2 | Science as Social Knowledge: Values and Objectivity in Scientific Inquiry | Longino (1990), Princeton University Press: develops contextual empiricism. Data support hypotheses only through background assumptions, so objectivity is secured not by individual method but by critical interaction in a community, and is a matter of degree. Applied to research on human evolution and neuroendocrinology. Unread: the account is read in Longino's SEP entry [LIT-725](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-725.md). | Unavailable — registered 2026-10-05 from Crossref, not read: no lawful full text could be reached (Princeton University Press via De Gruyter is closed). Its account is read first-hand in Longino's own Stanford Encyclopedia entry, "The Social Dimensions of Scientific Knowledge" ([LIT-725](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-725.md)), §5, which states the argument from underdetermination and the four community norms. Filed because an essay the owner is writing cites "Helen Longino's social epistemology" for institutionalized criticism. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied, not on merit. |
| [LIT-724](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-724.md) | The Communication Structure of Epistemic Communities | Zollman (2007), Philosophy of Science 74:574–587. Simulating Bala and Goyal's model, in which scientists learn only about the method they pursue, small communities connected in a cycle chose the better method more often than wheels or complete graphs, and took longer to do so. Over all networks of up to six agents, density predicted failure, and hub centrality did not. Misleading early results spread through dense networks before diversity could correct them. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-583](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-583.md)): read in full from the author's posted copy. Worth reading as the origin of the "Zollman effect". In a Bala–Goyal bandit model, where agents learn only about the method they pursue, simulated communities with fewer communication links converged on the better method more often and more slowly than fully connected ones. The cause was density, not the centrality of a hub. A simulation study of small networks (3–10 agents) at one payoff gap. [LIT-733](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-733.md) shows the effect is confined to hard inquiry. |
| [LIT-725](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-725.md) | The Social Dimensions of Scientific Knowledge | Longino, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (2002; rev. 2025). States her critical contextual empiricism: evidence bears on hypotheses only through background assumptions, so objectivity depends on critical interaction in a community. That interaction counts only if four norms hold: venues, uptake, public standards, and tempered equality of intellectual authority. It surveys rival models and reports that Zollman's network result is fragile. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-580](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-580.md)): §§1, 4 and 5 and the parts of §2 on network models, in the revision of 24 January 2025. Worth reading as Longino's own statement of her position, written by her as the entry's author, and as a survey of the rival models of social knowledge (Kitcher, Solomon, Zollman). Read §5 for critical contextual empiricism and its four community norms: venues for criticism, uptake of criticism, public standards, and tempered equality of intellectual authority. Being by Longino, its account of rivals is a participant's, not a neutral referee's. |
| [LIT-729](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-729.md) | Exploration and Exploitation in Organizational Learning | March (1991), Organization Science 2(1):71–87. Exploration's returns are less certain, more remote and more distant than exploitation's, so adaptive processes refine exploitation faster and become self-destructive in the long run. In a model of mutual learning, the organizational code improves only from members who deviate from it: slow socialization, mixed learning rates and moderate turnover raise organizational knowledge, at a cost to some individuals. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-581](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-581.md)): in full, from a JSTOR copy in an NTNU doctoral-course readings folder. Worth reading as the source of the exploration–exploitation trade-off in organizations: exploitation's returns are surer and nearer, so adaptation drives exploration out and becomes self-destructive. A simple simulation of mutual learning between members and an organizational code shows that slow socialization, a mix of learning rates and moderate turnover raise what the organization knows. Limits: the results are from simple models, and March gives no optimal balance. |
| [LIT-730](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-730.md) | Episteme Symposium on Group Agency: Replies to Gaus, Cariani, Sylvan, and Briggs | List & Pettit (2012), Episteme 9(3):293–309. Replies to a symposium on Group Agency. Ecological rationality is classical rationality relative to an environment; robust group rationality can be relaxed by context, yet proposition-wise aggregation stays very limited. Group attitudes are real and non-redundant: role-based member acceptance does not reduce them. Group agents are fit to be held responsible in their own right but should have restricted rights, on normative individualism. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-582](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-582.md)): in full, from the authors' copy on List's LSE pages. Worth reading as the authors' own short commentary on Group Agency ([LIT-391](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-391.md), unread), which it quotes with page references. It says the premise-based procedure was only ever illustrative, that robust group rationality may be relaxed case by case without rescuing proposition-wise supervenience, that no accessible individualistic recipe makes group attitudes redundant, and that group agents are fit to be held responsible in their own right but should have restricted rights. Limits: replies to commentaries not in the record; the book's claims are seen only as quoted. |
| [LIT-732](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-732.md) v2 | The Fate of Knowledge | Longino (2002), Princeton University Press: argues that the cognitive processes of science, observation and reasoning included, are social processes, so the community norms that make inquiry objective apply to the constructive work of research and not only to the criticism of its results. Unread: the thesis is read in Longino's SEP entry [LIT-725](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-725.md). | Unavailable — registered 2026-10-05 from Crossref, not read: no lawful full text could be reached (Princeton University Press via De Gruyter is closed). Longino's SEP entry ([LIT-725](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-725.md)) states its thesis: observation and reasoning are themselves social processes, so the community norms govern the constructive work of research and not only the review of finished results. Filed with [LIT-717](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-717.md) for the owner's essay. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied, not on merit. |
| [LIT-733](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-733.md) | In Epistemic Networks, Is Less Really More? | Rosenstock, Bruner & O'Connor (2017), Philosophy of Science 84:234–252. Replicating Zollman's models over wider parameters, the advantage of cycles over complete networks vanishes once the better action is slightly better (pB ≥ 0.525 at size 10), groups are larger, or agents gather more data per round. It persists only where inquiry is hard. Kummerfeld and Zollman's results behave the same way. Transient diversity is the robust lesson. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-559](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-559.md)): read in full from the copy on Cailin O'Connor's website. Worth reading as the robustness check on the Zollman effect. Over a wider parameter space, sparse networks beat dense ones only where inquiry is hard: small groups, small batches of data, and nearly indistinguishable alternatives. Elsewhere sparsity only slows learning. The authors keep Zollman's transient-diversity point as robust and read these models as "how-potentially" stories. |
| [LIT-735](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-735.md) | The Epistemic Benefit of Transient Diversity | Zollman (2010), Erkenntnis 72:17–35. In a richer bandit model with beta priors, sparse networks again beat dense ones. Making priors extreme reverses the order: dogmatic agents in a complete network do best. Both limited information and dogmatism keep diversity alive. Together they keep it alive too long, and agents fail to converge. The epistemic good is diversity that is transient. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-564](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-564.md)): read in full from the author's posted manuscript (dated 29 September 2009). Worth reading for its conclusion, which Rosenstock et al. ([LIT-733](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-733.md)) single out as the robust result of this literature: what a community needs is transient diversity, long enough to keep a theory from being dropped too soon and short enough to allow convergence. Sparse communication and stubborn priors each supply it, and together they make diversity too stable and learning fails. The peptic-ulcer history is the motivating case. |
| [LIT-744](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-744.md) | Experimentation by Industrial Selection | Holman & Bruner (2017), Philosophy of Science 84:1008–1019. Industry can bias a scientific community without corrupting anyone, by funding researchers whose methods already favour its product, so that they are more productive and train more newcomers. Shown in a bandit-model simulation with methodological diversity and turnover, after the antiarrhythmic drug case. An independent funder helps only if it discounts industry-funded work. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-574](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-574.md)): in full, from the publisher's PDF in ANU Open Research, the co-author's institutional repository, marked open access. Worth reading for a mechanism by which an outside funder biases a scientific community without corrupting anyone: given methodological diversity, a merit-based system and turnover, funding researchers whose methods already favour a product makes them more productive and more likely to train newcomers. An independent funder helps only if it discounts industry-funded work; funding on merit alone makes things worse. Limits: one historical case and a 20-agent simulation at a few parameter settings; run counts and network are not reported, and robustness to network structure rests on a footnote. |
| [LIT-751](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-751.md) v3 | The Problem of Intransigently Biased Agents | Holman & Bruner (2015), Philosophy of Science 82:956–968. By its abstract, one intransigently biased agent in Zollman's network model keeps an honest community from converging on the truth; two remedies are explored, one letting agents choose whom to trust. Unread: the authors' 2017 paper [LIT-744](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-744.md), read, applies the same model family to the same medical case. | Unavailable — registered 2026-10-05 from Crossref and the authors' institutional portals, not read: the published PDF in ANU Open Research is embargoed until 31 December 2037 and was not downloaded, the journal is closed, and no author-hosted copy was found. Only the abstract was seen: one intransigently biased agent in a Zollman network keeps an honest community from ever converging on the truth, and letting agents choose whom to trust is one remedy explored. The authors' 2017 paper "Experimentation by Industrial Selection" ([LIT-744](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-744.md)), read in full, uses the same model family on the same medical case and cites this one. Filed because it is the authors' first model of biased agents in medical research. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied, not on merit. |
| [LIT-794](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-794.md) | Making It Explicit: Reasoning, Representing, and Discursive Commitment | Brandom (1994), Harvard University Press. Explains meaning by use in normative terms. Asserting is undertaking a commitment, licensing others' reassertion and taking on responsibility to show entitlement; interlocutors keep score of one another's commitments and entitlements; a claim's content is its inferential role (what it follows from, what follows from it, what it rules out). Logical vocabulary makes these implicit proprieties explicit. Skimmed: the Preface and the core of chapter 3 only. | Active — skimmed 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-622](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-622.md)); the Preface and the core of chapter 3 (pp. 141–157 and 172–193) were read, the rest of the 741 pages not. Worth reading as the source of the deontic scorekeeping model of assertion. Asserting undertakes a commitment, authorizes others to reassert it, and takes on a responsibility to show entitlement if challenged. Every interlocutor keeps a score of everyone's commitments and entitlements, so the score is doubly perspectival, and an assertion's significance is the change it makes to each score, fixed by the content's inferential role. Read it with the caveat that the reading covers the model, not the book's arguments for it (chapters 1–2, 4–9). |
| [LIT-848](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-848.md) | Large AI models are cultural and social technologies | Farrell, Gopnik, Shalizi & Evans (2025), Science 387(6739):1153–1156, Policy Forum. Large models are best understood not as intelligent agents but as a new cultural and social technology: like writing, print and search they give access to what other people have produced, and like markets, bureaucracies and elections they make lossy, uninvertible summaries of it that can be operated on at scale. The questions that follow are the old ones about such technologies: homogenization or diversity, who gains and who loses, and which countervailing institutions emerge. Argued by historical analogy, without data. | Active — read in full 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-649](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-649.md)) from the authors' accepted version (Science galley of 25 February 2025, posted on Farrell's site); worth reading as the compact statement of the view that large models are not agents but a new cultural and social technology, of a kind with writing, print, markets, bureaucracies and elections: lossy summaries of what other humans have produced that let people reorganize it at scale. It is a four-page Policy Forum argued by analogy, with no data. Its one mechanism with consequences is that models fit their training distribution on average, so are least accurate where the data are rare, which may homogenize culture; it sets this against the possibility of "society-like" ecologies of models that keep diversity. |
| [LIT-900](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-900.md) v2 | The Method of Levels of Abstraction | Floridi (2008), DOI-10.1007/s11023-008-9113-7. Floridi gives up ontological levelism (levels in the system itself) and keeps an epistemological one, the method of levels of abstraction. An observable is an interpreted typed variable; an LoA is a finite non-empty set of observables; a moderated LoA adds a behaviour predicate; a gradient of abstractions (GoA) is a family of moderated LoAs with mutually inverse relations Rᵢ,ⱼ under which pⱼ ⇒ P_Rᵢ,ⱼ(pᵢ). Fixing the LoA fixes which questions can be asked and answered, and commits a theory to types (the LoA) and tokens (the model). The method is shown on Kant's antinomies, and set apart from Marr's, Pylyshyn's and Dennett's levels (which, it says, conceal their ontological commitment by privileging explanation), from Davidson's conceptual schemes, from relativism and from naive realism. It proves nothing about GoAs; its value is the vocabulary. | Active — read in full 2026-10-10 ([NOTE-700](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-700.md)); worth reading as the source statement of the method of levels of abstraction that Floridi's papers on agency, informational structural realism (LIT-152) and personal identity (LIT-136) all assume. Read §2 for the definitions, §2.7 for what an LoA commits a theory to, and §4.1 for the distinction between levels of abstraction, of organisation and of explanation. It is a method with definitions, not a result: no theorem is proved about GoAs, the one formal claim (disjoint and nested GoAs are interconvertible) does not go through under the paper's own definition of nestedness, and the guard against relativism (§4.3) is one paragraph that ranks LoAs only relative to a purpose. |
| [LIT-939](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-939.md) v2 | Modeling opinion misperception and the emergence of silence in online social system | Vilone and Polizzi (2024). In two agent-based models on scale-free networks with fixed private beliefs, a small hard-core minority makes expressed and perceived opinion lean far toward the minority. The first model has no voluntary silence. In the second, the majority falls silent: 55–60% of agents end silent, whatever the minority's size or degree. The network's direct (friendship-paradox) distortion of perception is small and of no fixed sign. Simulation only. No belief changes, and the majority is overturned in expression only above a minority of about 30%. | Active — read 2026-10-14 ([NOTE-810](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-810.md)) in full; worth reading for its separation of two sources of opinion misperception in a network: the friendship-paradox distortion of what members see, which it finds small and of no fixed sign, and a spiral of silence, which it finds large. With private beliefs held fixed, a hard-core minority drives 55–60% of agents into silence and makes expressed opinion lean far toward the minority. Read it knowing that it is simulation only, that no belief ever changes, and that the majority is overturned in expression only above a minority of about 30%. Filed for [QUESTION-047](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-047.md); [THEORY-242](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-242.md) holds what it shows. |
| [LIT-958](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-958.md) v2 | How manipulable are prediction markets? | Rasooly and Rozzi (2025). A pre-registered field experiment randomly moved prices by ±5 points in 817 Manifold prediction markets. About 25% of the yes–no gap reverted in the first week and 6% more over the next three. At 60 days, the last measurement, about 59% remained in unresolved markets. A model with finite, risk-averse traders predicts partial, slowing reversion even without learning. Markets with more traders, more activity or a Metaculus twin reverted more, but these splits are not randomised and are mostly significant only at 10%. | Active — read 2026-10-14 ([NOTE-778](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-778.md)) in full; worth reading as a randomised, pre-registered field experiment that answers the counterfactual question that historical manipulation studies could not. On 817 Manifold markets about 59% of a random ±5-point shock was still present after 60 days in unresolved markets, and a price-impact model with finite, risk-averse traders explains partial persistence even when no trader learns. Read it knowing that it cannot say whether traders came to believe the shocked price, that the platform runs mostly on play money, and that its evidence on which markets resist manipulation is correlational. Filed for [QUESTION-047](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-047.md); [THEORY-267](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-267.md) holds what it shows. |
| [LIT-966](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-966.md) v2 | Cooperative Dilemmas in Rational Debate | Handfield et al. (2025). Two debaters in a Betz-style logical space choose fixed argument strategies, with payoff w·v − d (true beliefs against changes of mind). At low and moderate truth weights the game is a cooperative dilemma: a prisoner's dilemma, stag hunt or, most often, a snowdrift in which one debater argues boldly and the other free-rides. At low weight both exit. At high weight in short debates mutual boldness is the unique, truth-optimal equilibrium. In a narrow band of mixed equilibria, raising the truth weight slightly lowers collective accuracy. All exact results are for n = 3 propositions. | Active — read 2026-10-14 ([NOTE-795](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-795.md)) in full; worth reading as a clean game-theoretic statement of epistemic free-riding in debate. Two deductive reasoners who value true beliefs but pay for each change of mind face a cooperative dilemma at low and moderate truth weights: typically one argues boldly and the other free-rides, and at low weights both exit. Read it knowing that it models two people and three propositions, that its outcome is collective accuracy and not a shared belief, and that the drop in accuracy as truth motivation rises is small and confined to a narrow band of mixed equilibria. Filed for [QUESTION-047](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-047.md); [THEORY-290](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-290.md) holds what it shows. |
| [LIT-988](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-988.md) v2 | Scientific discovery in a model-centric framework: Reproducibility, innovation, and epistemic diversity | Devezer et al. (2019). Scientists drawn at random test a proposed linear model against the consensus by AIC or SC, and the winner becomes the consensus. Markov-chain analysis and an agent-based model show that replication cannot change the transition matrix, so reproducibility cannot cause convergence. A population of boundary testers reproduces almost perfectly while rarely holding the true model. Strategies that keep the model space connected speed discovery. An equal mix of strategies is never the worst on any property and varies least, but it is not the best on time at the truth, and under high noise it fails too. | Active — read 2026-10-14 ([NOTE-792](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-792.md)) in full; worth reading for a formal model in which every inquiry step is a sound model comparison and the community's consensus still sits on a false model, with results that reproduce almost perfectly, because of which alternatives its research strategies put up. It proves that replication cannot change where the consensus goes. Read it knowing that the consensus is memoryless and held by no one, that its scientists neither believe nor learn, and that its "epistemic diversity optimizes" means only that an equal strategy mix is never the worst and varies least. Filed for [QUESTION-047](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-047.md); [THEORY-295](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-295.md) holds what it shows. |
| [LIT-999](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-999.md) v2 | Naïve Learning in Social Networks and the Wisdom of Crowds | Golub and Jackson (2010). Agents with independent noisy signals of a true value repeatedly average their neighbours' beliefs with fixed weights, ignoring repeated information. The consensus is the signals weighted by the network's left unit eigenvector, and in a growing society it converges to the truth if and only if the largest such influence weight vanishes; with reciprocal equal weights, if and only if no degree is a non-vanishing share of all links. A finite group everyone attends to prevents it; balance and dispersion conditions ensure it. Speed of consensus is unrelated to its correctness. | Active — read 2026-10-14 ([NOTE-840](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-840.md)) in full; worth reading for [QUESTION-047](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-047.md) as a proved case in which members share one updating rule and the network alone decides whether the group belief is right: a growing society of DeGroot averagers converges to the truth if and only if the largest influence weight vanishes. Read it knowing that its agents are naïve, not sound (they ignore repeated information), that weights are fixed and signals independent, and that the result is asymptotic and about a model, not data. |
| [LIT-1004](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1004.md) v3 | Epistemic Injustice: Power and the Ethics of Knowing | Fricker (2007). Names two kinds of wrong done to someone in her capacity as a knower. Testimonial injustice: a hearer gives a speaker a prejudicially deflated degree of credibility. Hermeneutical injustice: someone is handicapped in making sense of a social experience by a gap in collective understanding that is owed to the relative powerlessness of a social group she belongs to. Proposes testimonial and hermeneutical justice as corrective virtues of the hearer, each at once intellectual and ethical. Checked against the author's précis (2008), not the book. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-12 and read only in part: not the book but the author's own three-page précis of it (Theoria 23(1), 2008, pp. 69–71, DOI 10.1387/theoria.7, open access under CC BY-NC-ND), read in full in [NOTE-832](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-832.md) (Skimmed). The book itself was sought on 2026-10-14 and not reached. OpenAlex and Unpaywall report it closed, with no repository copy. Oxford Academic (academic.oup.com/book/32817, reached through the DOI) returned a bot check (403). PhilPapers returned 403, and no author-posted chapter was found. A full PDF on a Brazilian court library's repository (bdjur.stj.jus.br) carries the publisher's copyright notices and no sign of permission, so it was not used. The book's cases and arguments are therefore known here only as the précis states them. It stays Unavailable until a full copy is supplied ([ADR-041](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-041.md)): the search for one is recorded, and only a précis was read. It is the reading [QUESTION-072](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-072.md) was filed ahead of, and [THEORY-317](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-317.md) is filed from the précis. |
| [LIT-1007](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1007.md) v3 | The Ethics of Manipulation | Noggle, SEP (2018, revised 2026). A survey of ordinary manipulation. It sorts accounts of what manipulation is into bypassing reason (including the covert-influence view), trickery, pressure, and disjunctive, hybrid and non-definitional views, and gives a familiar tactic that breaks each single account. It finds manipulation neither wrong by definition nor absolutely, and sets out harm, autonomy, using a person's agency as a means, and infringed rights as candidate wrong-makers, each with its objection. It leaves open whether manipulation requires intent, including for algorithms that select their own means of influence. | Active — read 2026-10-14 ([NOTE-744](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-744.md)) in full; worth reading as the map of the philosophy of ordinary manipulation: what it is (bypassing reason, trickery, pressure, disjunctive, hybrid and non-definitional views, each with the case that breaks it) and why it is wrong when it is (harm, autonomy, using a person's agency as a means, rights). Its §4.2 states as open whether manipulation needs intent, with an algorithm that selects manipulative interface variants as its case, and lists five possible answers. Read it knowing that it is a survey that argues for little, that it is about ordinary rather than the free-will literature's global manipulation, and that the version read is the 2026 revision, not the 2018 text that Susser, Roessler and Nissenbaum cite. |
| [LIT-1021](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1021.md) v2 | Bayesian Persuasion | Kamenica & Gentzkow (2011), Am. Econ. Rev. 101(6): 2590–2615. With a common prior and a signal the receiver observes and the sender commits to, any distribution of posteriors that averages to the prior can be induced. The sender's best value is the concave closure of its value over posteriors, at the prior. A Bayesian judge who knows the investigation was designed to convict convicts 60 percent of defendants when 70 percent are innocent. At the optimum the receiver is certain when she takes the sender's worst action and indifferent otherwise. Blackwell is not cited and manipulation is not analysed. | Active — read in full 2026-10-13 (NOTE-717) from the published AER PDF posted on Gentzkow's Stanford faculty page (web.stanford.edu/~gentzkow/research/BayesianPersuasion.pdf); the online Appendix was not read. Registered at the owner's request from the survey of the Mathematics of Meaning corpus, for [QUESTION-070](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-070.md) and [QUESTION-071](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-071.md). Worth reading for the result that an overt, committed choice of experiment moves a fully informed Bayesian receiver, and for the optimum's signature: certainty when she takes the sender's worst action, indifference otherwise. It does not analyse manipulation and does not cite Blackwell. |
| [LIT-1046](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1046.md) | Powerlessness and Social Interpretation | Fricker (2006), Episteme 3(1–2):96–108, drawn from the final chapter of Epistemic Injustice. Hermeneutical injustice is "the injustice of having some significant area of one's social experience obscured from collective understanding owing to hermeneutical marginalization". It is systematic when the marginalisation is persistent and wide-ranging, and incidental when it is a one-off, localised moment of powerlessness, as for a socially powerful man whose stalking the police cannot hear. A gap with no marginalisation behind it, such as an undiagnosed illness, is bad luck, not injustice. The primary harm is situated hermeneutical inequality. Secondary harms include lost epistemic confidence and, at worst, the social construction of who the subject is. | Active — read 2026-10-14 ([NOTE-859](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-859.md)) in full; worth reading as Fricker's full statement of hermeneutical injustice, drawn by her own note from the book's final chapter: the definitions, systematic and incidental, the argument that a merely circumstantial gap is bad luck and not injustice, and the account of its primary and secondary harms. Its incidental case shows that, on her terms, hermeneutical injustice does not require membership of a powerless group, which the précis read for [LIT-1004](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1004.md) does not say. Filed as an alternative reading for [LIT-1004](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1004.md), whose book is Unavailable here. |
| [LIT-1048](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1048.md) | Evolving Concepts of Epistemic Injustice | Fricker (2017), Routledge Handbook of Epistemic Injustice, pp. 53–60. Her retrospective statement of the two concepts. Both are "discriminatory epistemic injustice": testimonial injustice is caused by a prejudice through which the speaker is ingenuously misjudged as epistemically lesser, and hermeneutical injustice by "hermeneutical marginalisation in relation to some area of social experience". She argues for keeping both strict about intention: a deliberate manipulation of credibility, or a hearer who pretends not to understand, is a related but different wrong. She accepts structural, pre-emptive testimonial injustice, as when an un-refreshed list of expert witnesses means some speakers are never asked. | Active — read 2026-10-14 ([NOTE-853](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-853.md)) in full; worth reading as Fricker's own later statement of both concepts, ten years after the book: testimonial injustice is an ingenuous, prejudiced misjudgement of a speaker and never a deliberate manipulation of credibility; hermeneutical injustice is caused by hermeneutical marginalisation and persists however earnestly hearers try; and both are "discriminatory" epistemic injustice, kept apart from distributive kinds. It also accepts Anderson's structural, pre-emptive testimonial injustice, in which a speaker's word is never sought because of an un-refreshed list. Filed as an alternative reading for [LIT-1004](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1004.md), whose book is Unavailable here. |
| [LIT-1049](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1049.md) | Epistemic Justice and a Role for Virtue in the Politics of Knowing | Fricker (2003), Metaphilosophy 34(1–2):154–173. A hearer can take someone's word critically without inference, through a testimonial sensibility: a socially trained, self-correcting capacity, like an ethical sensibility, in which stereotypes of credibility are a legitimate and needed heuristic. Where they carry prejudice, a speaker receives the wrong degree of credibility "owing to a certain sort of unintended prejudice on the hearer's part": testimonial injustice, shown in Tom Robinson's trial and in Greenleaf's dismissal of Marge. The corrective virtue, reflexive critical openness, corrects for the relation between the hearer's and the speaker's social identities. Its availability depends on the critical concepts of the hearer's time, so a hearer may be at fault before he is culpable. | Active — read 2026-10-14 ([NOTE-860](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-860.md)) in full; worth reading as Fricker's first statement of testimonial injustice and of the virtue that corrects it: a hearer's credibility judgements come from a socially trained testimonial sensibility, which stereotypes properly inform and prejudice can corrupt, so that a speaker gets "the wrong degree of credibility" through "unintended prejudice". It argues the corrective virtue is reflexive, and that whether a hearer can have it depends on the critical concepts available in their time. Filed as an alternative reading for [LIT-1004](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1004.md), whose book is Unavailable here. |

Worth reading as the source of the AGM postulates for contracting and revising a logically closed theory, of the Levi identity as the definition of revision, and of the two representation theorems: the six basic postulates characterize exactly the partial meet contractions (Observation 2.5), and with the two supplementary postulates exactly those generated by a transitive relation over the maximal non-implying subsets (Corollary 4.5). For [CLAIM-294](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-294.md) it shows that in AGM the closed theory alone does not fix a revision, since a selection function or ordering must be added and different ones disagree on the same theory, but the added state is a preference over remainders, not a record of what a belief depended on; the paper does not discuss why beliefs are held or the belief-base point, which belongs to Hansson ([LIT-1072](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1072.md)). For [QUESTION-105](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-105.md) it answers only a one-step version: a theory plus a transitive ordering suffices, with no redundancy in the finite case (Observation 4.6), and it says nothing about iterated revision. |
| [LIT-1072](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1072.md) | Logic of Belief Revision | Hansson's Stanford Encyclopedia survey of the logic of belief revision: AGM and its alternatives, and the contrast between revising logically closed belief sets and revising belief bases, which keep the beliefs held in their own right apart from their consequences. | Active — read in full 2026-10-15 from the Stanford Encyclopedia's own page (plato.stanford.edu/entries/logic-belief-revision/), the revision it dates "substantive revision Wed Jul 29, 2026", also served as the Fall 2026 archive edition. Worth reading as a compact, current survey of AGM belief revision and its rivals, and as the standard statement of why a belief base is not its closure: two bases with the same consequences are "statically equivalent" but not "dynamically equivalent", bases escape the Recovery postulate, and they keep inconsistent states apart where every closed set collapses to one. For [QUESTION-105](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-105.md) and [CLAIM-294](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-294.md) it shows the full-belief form of the claim that current conclusions are not a sufficient state for revision (the Abe and Bob example), and also that belief-set models carry the missing difference in a selection mechanism or entrenchment ordering instead of a base; for [CLAIM-295](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-295.md) its bases widen the operations that stay well defined but record only which beliefs are basic, not reasons, sources or defeated alternatives. Truth maintenance appears once, as history. The phrases "between belief states represented as closed sets" and "belief bases retaining additional structure" that the filing attributes via A10 are not in this revision. |
| [LIT-1182](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1182.md) v2 | An Introduction to QBism with an Application to the Locality of Quantum Mechanics | Fuchs, Mermin & Schack (2014). QBism: quantum states and all probabilities, 0 and 1 included, are an agent's personal judgements. A measurement is "any action an agent takes to elicit a set of possible experiences", and the outcome is the experience it elicits; it does not reveal a pre-existing state of affairs. The agent models everything external with quantum mechanics, other agents' reports included, and only her own awareness of her own experience is exempt. Quantum correlations are between one agent's time-like separated experiences, so the theory is local. | Active — read 2026-10-16 in full ([NOTE-955](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-955.md)), from the arXiv v1 PDF. Worth reading as the shortest authoritative statement of QBism: states and all probabilities, 1 included, are an agent's judgements, a measurement is an action the agent takes to elicit experience, and the outcome is that experience. Read it knowing that it keeps judgement (a state assignment) and measurement (an action on an external system) apart, so its loop is judgement, action, experience, update; and that the agent's own awareness is the one thing it does not model, so it has no measurement of the self. |

| [LIT-1269](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1269.md) | Intuitions about personal identity: An empirical study | Nichols & Bruno (2010), Philosophical Psychology 23:293–312. Survey studies of University of Arizona introductory philosophy students on Williams's (1970) personal-identity cases. A replication of Blok et al.'s brain-transplant vignette finds the person judged "still Jim" when memories survive and not when they are erased, in first- and third-person versions alike. A stripped-down version of Williams's Pain case (a brain infection treated by a procedure that eliminates "distinctive mental states") gets 68% (N = 50) saying "you will feel the pain" of later injections, and 72% (N = 54) in the third person, with no difference between the two. An open-ended abstract question draws psychological answers from over 70% (N = 53), and over 80% (N = 54) deny that a future person with none of their memories could be them. Given both and told they conflict, 64% (N = 45, p = 0.053) side with memory. The authors read the psychological intuitions as the more robust, and so as support for a psychological criterion "insofar as" intuitions should guide the theory. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-996](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-996.md)) in full, from the published PDF linked from the first author's own publications page; worth reading as the first survey test of Williams's two tellings of the body-exchange case and of his two explanations of why they diverge. Undergraduates mostly say a brain-transplant patient whose memories are erased is no longer the same person, and mostly say that a patient whose distinctive mental states are wiped will still feel the pain of later injections; neither result moves with first- against third-person telling. Asked abstractly, about 70% name psychological factors and more than 80% deny that someone without any of their memories could be them; made to choose, 64% side with memory (p = 0.053). Read it as evidence about how a concept of personal persistence responds to framing in one student population, not about what persistence is: the authors make the bearing conditional on intuitions informing the theory, test only necessity of psychology, and leave unseparated whether the Pain vignette asks about identity or about bare sentience. |

In network-epistemology models of scientists and policymakers, a propagandist who only selects and shares real, unbiased results that favour one side, without fabricating any, can lead policymakers to the false belief while the scientific community converges on the truth; so can one who runs honest studies and publishes only the favourable ones, best with the smallest studies; and a journalist who reports both sides equally slows policymakers' learning. | Active — read 2026-10-21 ([NOTE-1038](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1038.md)) in full, from the authors' arXiv manuscript (1801.01239v2); worth reading for its model of the tobacco strategy, in which selective sharing of genuine results and honest research published selectively mislead a Bayesian audience while the scientists converge on the truth ([THEORY-855](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-855.md)), for the conditions under which this works, and for the finding that 'fair' reporting slows the audience. Read it knowing that its policy makers update on forwarded results as if they were unselected, that every result is a simulation of a stylized bandit model averaged over runs in which the scientists reached the truth, and that why the smallest studies serve biased production best is a sufficient-statistic fact the paper does not state ([THEORY-845](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-845.md)). |

| [LIT-1360](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1360.md) v2 | Real patterns, the predictive mind, and the cognitive construction of the manifest image | Gładziejewski (2025), Synthese 206:225. Dennett's compression criterion for real patterns is carried through minimum description length, Bayesian inference and variational free energy, so learning a generative model is real-pattern extraction from sensory data. The manifest image is then a structural description of the sensory signal, equally veridical for an envatted twin with matched input. Applied to selves: a self-model compresses self-generated regularities by positing one common cause, real as a pattern, not as a substance, and the realism dispute is over criteria. Applied to objects: compression-based composition (Bird 2023) favours cats over arbitrary sums. | Active — read in full 2026-10-22 ([NOTE-1056](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1056.md)) from the publisher's open-access PDF (Springer, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0); worth reading as a clear derivation of Dennett's real patterns into predictive processing, through minimum description length and the complexity–accuracy split of free energy, and as a short diagnosis of the realism dispute about selves: a self-model compresses self-generated regularities by positing one common cause, so the self is real as a pattern and not as a substance, and the dispute is over criteria. The structural, Kantian realism it draws (the manifest image is veridical in a matched vat) needs manifest content to be wholly structural, which it assumes. It says nothing about consciousness, and it does not say a self-model exaggerates the self's unity. |

A formal account of memory for persistent agents whose central requirement is "revision sufficiency": retained state must support a declared family of future questions, interventions and changes of evaluative law. It characterizes exact revision sufficiency for finite histories by a factorization condition, derives a lower bound on representation size, and proposes an architecture that keeps grounds and counterevidence with each commitment. | Active — read in full 2026-10-22 ([NOTE-1091](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1091.md)) from the web page, version 4.0 of 25 September 2026, with its PDF and reproducibility archive, whose checks were run and reproduce; worth reading as a careful, self-limiting formal statement of what a reduced memory must keep for an agent to stay able to revise: exact sufficiency for a declared family of future demands is factorization through the retained state (the record's [CLAIM-350](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-350.md)), and under repeated declared revisions it is the coarsest revision-invariant refinement (Moore–Nerode), filed as [THEORY-884](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-884.md). Elementary and, by its authors' account, a synthesis; its architecture and experiment are proposals, unexecuted. It is the closest outside statement of [CLAIM-295](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-295.md) and answers [QUESTION-112](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-112.md) only for a revision family declared in advance. | [LIT-1518](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1518.md) | Eliciting Informative Feedback: The Peer-Prediction Method | Miller, Resnick & Zeckhauser (2005). A center with no independent information scores each rater by applying a strictly proper scoring rule to the distribution of a reference rater's report that her own report implies, given a common prior and signal model. Truthful reporting is a strict Nash equilibrium; scaling the scores induces costly effort and can outweigh bribes; three or more raters allow budget balance. Uninformative equilibria also exist, and collusion, risk aversion, unmodelled private signals and trust in the center are named limits. | Active — read in full 2026-10-24 ([NOTE-1139](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1139.md)) from the authors' final pre-publication draft of 26 January 2005, on Paul Resnick's University of Michigan page; worth reading as the founding scoring rule for evaluators when there is no ground truth. Each rater reports a signal, the center turns it into a posterior over a reference rater's report, and the rater is paid a strictly proper scoring rule on that posterior against what the reference rater actually reported. Truth-telling is then a strict Nash equilibrium (Proposition 1), and scaling the payments buys effort. It is not the only equilibrium: everyone always reporting h, or always l, is an equilibrium too, and collusion is named as a limit the paper does not settle. The mechanism needs a common prior and a signal model the center knows. |
